issues.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may be held vicariously liable for a killing committed by one member when the killing furthered the assembly’s common object or was an offence the members knew was likely to be committed in pursuit of that object.
material_facts: The prosecution evidence accepted by the courts showed that more than five persons assembled with the principal assailant and came armed with lethal weapons.
The principal assailant shot and killed the deceased and also shot at the deceased’s brother.
The weapons carried and the group’s conduct supported the finding that the assembly shared an object of attacking the deceased and his brother and knew that the fatal attack was likely.
issues.conclusion: The appellants were rightly convicted for the killing with the aid of Section 149 IPC.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 IPC imposes vicarious liability where an offence is committed in prosecution of an unlawful assembly’s common object or is an offence its members knew was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. A prior meeting of minds or an overt act by every member is not necessary; the common object and members’ knowledge may be inferred from the assembly’s conduct, weapons, and surrounding circumstances. The Court relied on Mizaji v. State of U.P., Masalti v. State of U.P., and Pandurang Chandrakant Mhatre v. State of Maharashtra.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenges_common_object_conviction and unlawful_assembly_has_at_least_five_members and members_carry_lethal_weapons and attack_furthers_shared_object and members_know_fatal_offence_is_likely

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenges_common_object: The accused appeal a criminal conviction imposed on them through liability for an offence committed by another member of an assembly.
predicates.unlawful_assembly_has_at_least_five_memb: At least five people acted together as an unlawful assembly.
predicates.members_carry_lethal_weapons: Members of the assembly arrived or acted while carrying lethal weapons.
predicates.attack_furthers_shared_object: The fatal attack was connected to and furthered the object shared by the assembly.
predicates.members_know_fatal_offence_is_likely: The assembly’s weapons and conduct showed that its members knew a fatal offence was likely to be committed in pursuit of their object.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a conviction based on an assembly’s common object, and the assembly had at least five members who carried lethal weapons, furthered a shared object through the attack, and knew a fatal offence was likely, the vicarious conviction for that offence is sustained.

issues.legal_issue: The right of private defence does not justify a fatal attack where the accused were the aggressors and faced no imminent danger requiring defensive force.
material_facts: The deceased was cleaning disputed land and had only a broomstick; the evidence showed that he committed no overt act and posed no threat to the accused or their property.
The accused arrived with the principal assailant, carrying lethal weapons, and the principal assailant shot the deceased and his brother.
The courts found that the accused were the aggressors and that there was no necessity to use force to avert an imminent danger.
issues.conclusion: The appellants failed to establish a right of private defence, and their claim was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 96 and 97 IPC recognize private defence of the body and property, subject to the restrictions in Section 99; Section 100 permits causing death only in specified circumstances, including an assault reasonably causing apprehension of grievous hurt. Under Sections 102 and 105, the right begins when a reasonable apprehension of danger arises and continues while it lasts. Private defence is defensive, not aggressive or retaliatory, and the force used must not be unduly disproportionate. The accused bear the burden of establishing the plea on a balance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt. The Court relied on Jai Dev v. State of Punjab, Laxman Sahu v. State of Orissa, Dharam v. State of Haryana, Vidhya Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and the other authorities cited in its discussion.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_raises_private_defence and accused_party_are_aggressors and no_imminent_danger_to_body_or_property and accused_use_fatal_force

predicates.criminal_appeal_raises_private_defence: The accused appeal a criminal conviction and rely on a claim that their conduct was defensive.
predicates.accused_party_are_aggressors: The accused initiated or escalated the violence rather than responding defensively to an attack.
predicates.no_imminent_danger_to_body_or_property: The accused faced no imminent threat of harm to a person or property that required immediate defensive action.
predicates.accused_use_fatal_force: The accused used force that caused a person’s death.

issues.definition: A private-defence claim is rejected when, in a criminal appeal raising that claim, the accused were the aggressors, faced no imminent danger to a person or property, and used fatal force.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to explain an accused person’s injuries does not by itself invalidate its case when the injuries are not serious and the prosecution evidence is cogent and credible.
material_facts: One accused had swelling and a fracture of the underlying bone in his upper arm, along with a complaint of shoulder pain.
The Court characterized the injuries as simple and superficial and found the evidence against the appellants cogent and creditworthy.
The prosecution had not explained the accused person’s injuries.
issues.conclusion: The unexplained injuries did not undermine the prosecution case or warrant setting aside the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: There is no absolute rule that the prosecution must explain every injury sustained by an accused in the same occurrence or that failure to do so requires rejection of the prosecution case. Under Takhaji Hiraji v. Thakore Kubersing Chamansing, non-explanation may affect the prosecution case when the accused’s injury was serious and was caused during the occurrence in question. The Court also held that cogent and creditworthy prosecution evidence may outweigh the omission to explain injuries.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenges_conviction: The accused appeal a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_sustained_unexplained_injury_in_: An accused person was injured in the incident and the prosecution did not explain that injury.
predicates.injury_is_not_serious: The accused person’s injury was simple or superficial rather than serious.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_is_cogent_and_credi: The evidence supporting the prosecution case was cogent and creditworthy.

issues.definition: A conviction is not set aside for an unexplained injury when an accused appeals a conviction, sustained an unexplained injury in the incident, and either the injury was not serious or the prosecution evidence was cogent and credible.
